fig:cassini.title: Level sets of $f(x,y)=(x^2+y^2)^2-2(x^2-y^2)$. Below the critical value $0$ (charcoal) each level is two ovals around the minima at $(\pm 1,0)$; above it (ochre) one oval. Exactly at the critical value the level set is the lemniscate (coral), which has a crossing at the saddle point $(0,0)$ and is not a manifold there. The marked points are the three critical points, where $f$ takes the critical values $-1$, $0$ and $-1$

fig:arm.title: A two-link arm with $\ell _1=1$ and $\ell _2=0.6$, anchored at the origin, reaches the point $w$ in two ways, elbow up and elbow down. Its workspace is the shaded annulus $\ell _1-\ell _2\le |w|\le \ell _1+\ell _2$. The two boundary circles are exactly the critical values of the arm map of Exercise~\ref {ex:twolinkarm}: there, the two solutions merge and the arm loses a direction of motion

fig:torusflow.title: An orbit of the constant field $(1,\alpha )$ on the torus, with $\alpha =\frac {\sqrt 5-1}2$, drawn in the unit square whose opposite sides are glued (as the arrows indicate). The orbit starts at the rust dot and darkens with time. It never closes, and in the long run it fills the square uniformly

thm:bracketloop.title: the bracket as a small loop

fig:bracketloop.title: The loop of Theorem~\ref {thm:bracketloop} for $X=\frac \partial {\partial x}$ and $Y=x\frac \partial {\partial y}$ in the plane, with $p=(0.6,0)$ and $s=0.6$. Moving right, the vertical flow is stronger, so the upward step $s(x+s)$ exceeds the downward step $sx$ taken after moving back. The loop misses by exactly $s^2[X,Y]=s^2\frac \partial {\partial y}$ (Exercise~\ref {ex:noncommute})

fig:boundary.title: A compact plane region $M$ with one hole, a manifold with boundary. With the standard orientation of the plane, the induced orientation of $\partial M$ runs anticlockwise on the outer curve and clockwise on the inner one: in both cases the outward normal (coral) followed by the direction of the boundary is a positive basis

ex:sigma.title: the volume form of the sphere

thm:h1punctured.title: de Rham's theorem for the punctured plane

cor:windingintegral.title: the winding number as an integral

fig:shoelace.title: The shoelace formula. Each edge $pq$ of the polygon, traversed anticlockwise, contributes the signed area $\frac 12\det (p,q)$ of the triangle $0pq$: positive (ochre) when the edge turns anticlockwise around the origin, negative (rust) otherwise. Where triangles of both signs overlap they cancel, and what remains is the polygon

fig:index.title: Three isolated zeros. Going once around the coral circle anticlockwise, the arrow turns once anticlockwise for the source $(x,y)$, once clockwise for the saddle $(x,-y)$, and twice anticlockwise for the field $z^2=(x^2-y^2,2xy)$. Their indices are $+1$, $-1$ and $+2$

thm:torusspectrum.title: the spectrum of the square flat torus

fig:girard.title: A spherical triangle $ABC$ on the unit sphere, with the three great circles that carry its sides. Its angles add up to more than $\pi $; the excess is its area

fig:helix.title: The covering $\R \to S^1$ drawn as a helix over the circle. A loop that goes twice around the circle lifts to a path that climbs two turns of the helix: the height it gains is the number of turns, and no homotopy of the loop can change it

fig:coverings.title: The figure eight $R_2$, with loops $a$ (coral) and $b$ (charcoal), and its three connected two-sheeted coverings. Each vertex has exactly one outgoing and one incoming edge of each colour; reading edge labels along loops at the lower vertex gives the subgroup of index $2$: $\langle a,\,b^2,\,bab^{-1}\rangle $, $\langle b,\,a^2,\,aba^{-1}\rangle $ and $\langle a^2,\,ab,\,b^2\rangle $, each free of rank $3$

fig:torustriang.title: A triangulation of the torus: a $3\times 3$ grid of squares, each cut by a diagonal, with opposite sides of the big square glued (the vertex labels show the gluing). It has $V=9$, $E=27$, $F=18$, and $V-E+F=0$. A coarser grid would not do: with a $2\times 2$ grid, two different triangles would have the same three vertices

fig:mvsphere.title: Mayer--Vietoris on the sphere: two open caps $U_+$ and $U_-$, each contractible, overlap in a band that retracts onto the equator. A cycle on $S^n$ is the sum of a chain in $U_+$ and a chain in $U_-$; its image under $\delta $ is their common boundary, a cycle in the band, one dimension lower. So every sphere carries exactly one hole, in its top dimension

fig:ballmodel.title: $SO(3)$ as a ball of radius $\pi $: the point $\theta u$ is the rotation by $\theta $ about $u$, and antipodal points of the boundary sphere are glued (a rotation by $\pi $ about $u$ equals one about $-u$). Left: a full turn about an axis is a diameter, a closed loop that cannot be shrunk; its two ends are glued, and moving one end drags the other to the opposite side. Right: two turns are two diameters; rotating the second one until it meets the first, then pulling the pair inwards, shrinks the loop to a point. This is Dirac's belt trick

thm:torus.title: maximal torus and Weyl group of $U(n)$

thm:haarform.title: Haar measure of a matrix Lie group

thm:correlations.title: correlation functions of random unitary matrices

fig:cue.title: Left: the $24$ eigenvalues of a Haar random matrix of $U(24)$, sampled as in Theorem~\ref {thm:qrhaar}. Middle: $24$ independent uniform points. The eigenvalues are spread more evenly; the independent points form clumps and leave gaps. Right: the pair correlation $1-(\frac {\sin \pi u}{\pi u})^2$ of Corollary~\ref {cor:dyson}, against the constant $1$ of independent points; near $u=0$ it behaves like $\frac {\pi ^2}3u^2$

geometry:fig:halfplane.title: Left: the h-line $x^2+y^2=1$ (charcoal) and three h-lines through $P$ that never meet it (rust). Right: the region above the unit circle between $x=\cos (\pi -\alpha )$ and $x=\cos \beta $ is a triangle with angles $\alpha $, $\beta $ and $0$ (its third vertex is at infinity)

thm:geodflow.title: the geodesic flow is a matrix product

fig:modular.title: The tessellation of $\mathbb H$ by the images of the fundamental domain $F$ (shaded) under $SL_2(\Z )$. The tiles accumulate at every rational point of the real axis; each is a hyperbolic triangle of area $\frac \pi 3$, and they are all congruent, however small some of them look

fig:farey.title: The Farey tessellation (edges between Farey neighbours, here with denominators up to $12$) and the h-line from $1-\sqrt 2$ to $1+\sqrt 2=[2;2,2,\dots ]$. After crossing the edge from $0$ to $\infty $ it passes two triangles with the vertex $\infty $ on its left, then two with a vertex on its right, and so on: the cutting sequence $LLRRLLRR\cdots $

fig:squaremap.title: A Riemann map made explicit: $f(z)=\int _0^z\frac {\dd w}{\sqrt {1+w^4}}$ maps the unit disc onto a square (a Schwarz--Christoffel integral). The images of the circles $|z|=0.2,0.4,\dots ,0.99$ and of sixteen radii, computed from the power series $f(z)=\sum _k\binom {-1/2}k\frac {z^{4k+1}}{4k+1}$. Angles are preserved everywhere inside; at the four corners, images of the points where $w^4=-1$, the right angles of the square are created from the straight angle of the circle

thm:linesunique.title: uniqueness of the measure on lines

fig:crofton.title: Left: random lines for the invariant measure, among those meeting a disc, and a curve inside it; the crossings are marked. Averaged over many lines, the number of crossings is $\frac {2L}{2\pi R}$ by Crofton's formula, where $2\pi R$ is the measure of the lines meeting the disc. Right: a Reuleaux triangle between pairs of parallel support lines, at the same distance $w$ in every direction

geometry:fig:tworeflections.title: A reflection in $m_1$ followed by a reflection in $m_2$ is the rotation about their intersection by twice the angle $\varphi $ from $m_1$ to $m_2$ (Exercise~\ref {geometry:ex:chasles})

geometry:fig:friezes.title: The seven frieze patterns, each obtained by applying a frieze group to one L-shaped tile. The dotted line is the axis. The step is the trail of a walker, the jump that of someone jumping with feet together

geometry:fig:lattices.title: The five types of plane lattices, with point groups $C_2$, $D_2$, $D_2$, $D_4$, $D_6$. In the centred rectangular lattice the rectangle spanned by $a$ and $b$ has a lattice point at its centre

geometry:fig:euler.title: The Euler line through the circumcentre, the centroid and the orthocentre, with the centroid twice as far from the orthocentre as from the circumcentre, and the nine-point circle of half the circumradius

geometry:fig:steiner.title: A Steiner chain of seven circles. It is the image, under an inversion, of a ring of seven equal circles between two concentric circles, which is why it closes up wherever it starts

geometry:fig:pappus.title: The Pappus chain in an arbelos. The centre of $C_n$ is exactly $n$ diameters of $C_n$ above the line $AB$ (rust), as the computation from the inverted picture confirms

geometry:thm:descartes.title: Descartes 1643, Soddy 1936; Lagarias, Mallows and Wilks 2002

geometry:fig:gasket.title: The Apollonian gasket with root quadruple $(-1,2,2,3)$: the outer circle has radius $1$, the two large circles radius $\frac 12$, and every circle has an integer curvature. The circles of curvature $6$ come from $2\cdot (-1+2+3)-2$

geometry:fig:floor.title: A tiled floor seen from a height. The picture is the image of the floor under a projective map. The parallel edges of the tiles meet at the central vanishing point, the diagonals at two others, and all three lie on the horizon, the image of the line at infinity

geometry:fig:desargues.title: Desargues' theorem. The triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are in perspective from $O$; the intersections $P,Q,R$ of corresponding sides lie on one line (rust)

geometry:fig:pappus4.title: Pappus' theorem. The three crossing points $X,Y,Z$ of the ``wrong'' pairs of lines are collinear

geometry:fig:fano.title: The Fano plane $\mathbb P^2(\mathbb F_2)$. The seven lines are the six segments and the circle; each line has three points, and three points form a line when their coordinates add up to $0$ modulo $2$

geometry:fig:dandelin.title: Dandelin's spheres, seen from the side. The cutting plane (charcoal) meets the cone in an ellipse; the two spheres inscribed in the cone and tangent to the plane touch it at the foci $F_1$ and $F_2$

geometry:fig:pascal.title: Pascal's hexagram. The hexagon $ABCDEF$ is inscribed in an ellipse; the meeting points $X,Y,Z$ of opposite sides lie on the Pascal line

geometry:fig:polar.title: The polar of $P$ (rust) passes through the points of contact $T_1,T_2$ of the tangents from $P$. On every line through $P$ that cuts the conic at $M$ and $N$, the polar cuts at the harmonic conjugate $Q$ of $P$

geometry:fig:poncelet.title: Poncelet triangles. The circles have radii $R=1$ and $r=0.36$, and the distance between their centres satisfies $d^2=R^2-2Rr$. Three starting points give three triangles, each inscribed in the outer circle and circumscribed about the inner one

geometry:fig:lorentz.title: The level sets of the form $x^2+y^2-t^2$, of signature $(2,1)$: the value $1$ gives a hyperboloid of one sheet, $0$ the light cone and $-1$ a hyperboloid of two sheets

geometry:fig:hyperboloid.title: The hyperboloid of one sheet $x^2+y^2-z^2=1$ with its two families of lines. Through $(\cos \theta ,\sin \theta ,0)$ pass the lines with directions $(-\sin \theta ,\cos \theta ,\pm 1)$

geometry:fig:saddle.title: The saddle $z=xy$ is ruled twice: by the lines $x=c,\ z=cy$ (charcoal) and $y=c,\ z=cx$ (rust)

geometry:fig:singular.title: Singular cubics: a node $y^2=x^2(x+1)$, a cusp $y^2=x^3$, and the folium of Descartes $x^3+y^3=3xy$, whose node is at the origin. The singular points are in rust

geometry:thm:bezout.title: B\'ezout, with multiplicities relative to a point $O$; the intrinsic form is proved in Volume~13, Chapter~14

geometry:fig:bezout.title: The circle $x^2+y^2=3.24$ and the cubic $y=x^3-3x$ meet in $6=2\times 3$ points, the most B\'ezout's theorem allows

geometry:fig:pascalcb.title: Pascal by Cayley--Bacharach. The charcoal cubic $AB\cup CD\cup EF$ and the rust cubic $BC\cup DE\cup FA$ meet in nine points. The conic together with the line $XY$ is a cubic through eight of them, so it contains the ninth, $Z$

geometry:fig:bachet.title: Bachet's tangent on $y^2=x^3-2$. The tangent at $P=(3,5)$, of slope $\frac {27}{10}$, meets the curve again at $P*P=\bigl (\frac {129}{100},\frac {383}{1000}\bigr )$; reflecting in the $x$-axis gives the point $2P$ of Section~\ref {geometry:sec:weierstrass}

geometry:thm:assoc.title: associativity for nine distinct points; for all triples it is proved in Volume~13, Chapter~15

geometry:fig:realcubics.title: Two real cubics: $y^2=x^3-x$ has two components, $y^2=x^3-x+1$ has one. The rust points are the real inflection points in the affine plane; with the point at infinity $O$ they are the three points of the vertical dashed line (Theorem~\ref {geometry:thm:realflexes})

geometry:fig:hesse.title: The Hesse configuration: nine points, twelve lines of three points each, any two points on exactly one line. Eight lines are straight; the four other ones are drawn as circles

geometry:fig:finitecubic.title: The $99$ affine points of $y^2=x^3-x+1$ over $\mathbb F_{101}$; with $O$, $E(\mathbb F_{101})$ has $100$ points, and $|100-102|=2\le 2\sqrt {101}$

geometry:fig:packings.title: Disks of diameter $1$ centred at the points of the square lattice and of the hexagonal lattice. In rust, a fundamental parallelogram: each contains exactly one disk's worth of area, $\frac \pi 4$, and has area $1$ for the square lattice and $\frac {\sqrt 3}2$ for the hexagonal one

geometry:fig:twosquares.title: The proof of Theorem~\ref {geometry:thm:twosquares} for $p=13$, $m=5$: the lattice $b\equiv 5a\pmod {13}$ and the disk $a^2+b^2<26$. The four rust points are $\pm (2,-3)$ and $\pm (3,2)$, and $13=2^2+3^2$

geometry:fig:reduction.title: Two bases of the same lattice: a long thin one (rust) and the reduced one found by Gauss's algorithm (ochre). Both parallelograms have the same area

geometry:fig:e8.title: The $240$ shortest vectors of $E_8$, projected onto a well-chosen plane (the \emph {Coxeter plane}): they fall on eight circles of $30$ points each

geometry:fig:sphere.title: The spherical triangle with vertices $e_1,e_2,e_3$ has three right angles. Its area is $\frac {3\pi }2-\pi =\frac \pi 2$, one eighth of the sphere

geometry:fig:tiling.title: The Poincar\'e disk tiled by hyperbolic triangles with angles $\frac \pi 2$, $\frac \pi 3$, $\frac \pi 7$, alternately coloured. All the triangles are congruent: they only look smaller near the boundary, which is infinitely far away

geometry:fig:buffon.title: Forty needles of length $0.8$ thrown on lines at distance $1$. Here $20$ of them cross a line (in rust); the theorem predicts a proportion $\frac {1.6}\pi \approx 0.51$

geometry:fig:reuleaux.title: A Reuleaux triangle and a disk of constant width $1$, each turning inside a unit square while touching its four sides. Both have perimeter $\pi $

geometry:fig:minkowskisum.title: The Minkowski sum of a triangle $A$ (area $1.4$) and a square $B$ (area $0.49$) is a hexagon of area $4.27$, and $\sqrt {4.27}\approx 2.07\ge \sqrt {1.4}+\sqrt {0.49}\approx 1.88$

geometry:fig:vertices.title: The ellipse $x=1.6\cos t$, $y=\sin t$ with its osculating circles at the four vertices (radius $0.625$ at the ends of the long axis, $2.56$ at the ends of the short one), and its curvature as a function of $t$: two maxima and two minima

geometry:fig:defect.title: The three squares at a corner of a cube, unfolded into the plane, leave a gap of $\frac \pi 2$: the angular defect. The cube has eight corners, and $8\cdot \frac \pi 2=4\pi $
